title: What happens to the red petals when the rangoli turns?
description: A round rangoli with a ring in the centre and four red petals is turned by ninety degrees about its centre. The petals land on one another and the picture looks the same. Keeko's doubt is that the rangoli looks different after the turn.
teaching_notes: One idea: when a figure with equal parts is turned by the right angle about its centre, each part lands where another part was, so the picture repeats. Watch for students who think the picture changes because the parts have moved.

source: Look at the rangoli picture (a round flower-like design with
video_script.why: The child sees that a quarter turn about the centre sends each red petal onto the next one, so the rangoli looks the same and its pattern repeats.
video_script.substitution: Turn the rangoli by a quarter turn about its centre; each petal lands where the next petal was.
video_script.anchor: a round rangoli with a ring in the centre and four red petals around it
video_script.wrong_answer: the rangoli looks different after the turn
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the rangoli looks different after the turn, because every petal has moved. Comparing it with the faint start picture shows the two look exactly alike, because each petal landed where another petal used to be.
video_script.payoff_line: The red petals come back onto themselves after a quarter turn

final_answer.value: The same petal shape repeats around the centre; turned by 90 degrees about the centre, the red petals come back exactly onto themselves
final_answer.spoken: turned by ninety degrees, the red petals come back exactly onto themselves

maths_rules: To rotate a figure is to turn it about a fixed point, the centre
A full turn is 360 degrees; a quarter of a full turn is 360 / 4 = 90 degrees
4 red petals share a full turn, so the gap from one petal to the next is 360 / 4 = 90 degrees
A turn of 90 degrees sends each petal onto the next petal, so the rangoli overlaps its start picture
video_script.design: One idea: a quarter turn about the centre sends each petal onto the next, so the rangoli repeats. The rangoli stays on the board all video. Wrong idea: the picture changes because the petals moved.
